title: AI stock sell-off sparks a new debate over the data-center buildout
excerpt: Election fallout is forcing investors to rethink AI spending, debt risk, and which companies can weather a slower buildout.
content_html:
The AI trade got a harsh reminder Thursday that its biggest risk may not be whether artificial intelligence works.

It may be whether America can — or wants to — build enough data centers to make it work.

While the stock-market carnage was deep and spared no major sectors, AI-linked tech felt the pain to an outsized degree. The Nasdaq 100 plunged more than 6% for its worst day since 2020. Within the AI trade, chipmakers and neoclouds — both central to the AI-infrastructure buildout — were standout losers.

The jitters are straightforward: Political backlash against data centers could slow the construction boom that's kept the AI trade humming.

But there are two very different ways to interpret that risk, which has fueled a mounting debate: Is a slowdown a direct blow to AI's biggest growth engine, or a needed cooling-off period that could help prevent a bubble?

The negative case: The AI boom hits a wall

The immediate argument is not complicated. If Democrats use their new influence to do things like tighten permitting, scrutinize power and water usage, or curb tax incentives, then fewer data centers get built. And the ones that do take longer and cost more.

That hits the AI supply chain from the bottom up. Chipmakers lose orders. Power-equipment suppliers lose projects. Data-center developers — especially the ones heavily reliant on debt financing — have a harder time justifying their massive spending plans.

And it comes at an already-fragile moment for the AI trade. Even before the election, investors were starting to question capex bills and gravitate towards "quality" companies with strong finances. A policy-driven delay only injects more uncertainty.

UBS has gone as far as to put a number on it. They project that roughly 30% of expected data center additions in 2028 could be impacted by construction pauses.

The positive case: Near-term pain for long-term gain

This is where it gets really interesting. What if slowing down the AI buildout ends up being a … good thing?

The thinking goes that a slower, more expensive buildout could help ease fears of an AI bubble. It's been a popular narrative as the AI trade has exploded higher, with skeptics arguing that supply will eventually outrun real demand.

If the buildout slows down, hyperscalers could have more time to show investors tangible results from their capex spending. Developers may also be forced to be pickier about which projects get built. In theory, those developments could help silence the haters and bubble-mongers.

It could also intensify the flight to quality already playing out in the stock market. The companies that can fund their own power and absorb delays, without having to tap debt markets, will be well-positioned. In other words, quality companies look attractive in both the negative and positive scenarios.

Thursday's market action made clear which side investors favor right now: The blue wave looks like a fresh threat to the AI trade.

But a slower buildout is not necessarily the same thing as a broken one. If it turns a capex arms race into a more disciplined race to prove returns, today's political roadblock could look less like a wall, and more like a guardrail.
